learn.title: Learn English Concepts

content.text: In English we have several tenses. In the present tense we may say, "We go to college."
In the past we say, "We went to college."
In the future we say, "We will go to college."

learn.title: Learn Future Indicative Verbs

content.text: In the present tense in Greek we have seen that aspect, rather than time, is the focus. The future tense in Greek specifies that the action of the verb takes place in the future. This is similar to the future tense in English. Summers notes three functions of the future tense in Greek (p. 67):

items: deliberative with rhetorical questions (e.g. "to whom shall we go?").

content.text: The future tense is easy to remember as the endings are the same as the present. The difference is a sigma which is usually added between the stem and the ending.

Stem + Sigma + Ending
λύ + σ + ω
(λύσω — I will loose)
The future passive will be learned later as it is built off a different stem.
The adding of the sigma may change the final consonant of the verb stem in the following three ways:

items:
if after a [[link:palatal]]palatal[[/link]] ( κ, γ, χ )
σ + [ κ, γ, χ] ==> ξ

if after a [[link:labial]]labial[[/link]] ( π, β, φ )
σ + [ π, β, φ] ==> ψ

if after a [[link:dental]]dental[[/link]] ( τ, δ, θ )
σ + [ τ, δ, θ ] ==> σ
if after a [[link:liquid]]liquid[[/link]] ( λ, μ, ν, ρ ) the sigma is dropped and the ω is accented with a circumflex. When a stem ends in a double liquid consonant, one of them is sometimes dropped.
if after a [[link:sibilant]]sibilant[[/link]] ( σ, ζ ) the sibilant is dropped and the sigma is kept.

content.text: Quite frequently there are verbs which in the present tense are not deponent but in the future they are:
Sometimes the future stem is totally different from the original present stem. Thus when you learn verbs in the future you should learn both stem roots.
